newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission meets on four or six new EU members.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission meets on four or six new EU members.

text.p: The European Commission met on Thursday for a crucial session which could decide the fate of Estonia and Slovenia's ambitions to join a first eastwards expansion of the European Union.

Divided over whether the bloc's first foray behind the former Iron Curtain should embrace just the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland, along with Cyprus, or also Estonia and Slovenia the EU executive was also to discuss what kind of waiting room should be created for countries left out.

The EU's External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek was to present the 20 commissioners with detailed assessments of how suitable 10 eastern countries are for the economic and political rigours of EU membership.
Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Bulgaria and Romania have also applied for entry and have been heavily lobbying for talks to start with all at the same time.

Although Van den Broek has strong backing for his plan to extend to five eastern countries in the first instance, powerful forces in the Commission surrounding Commission President Jacques Santer want a smaller expansion to avoid an EU institutional overhaul.

The Commission will take a final decision on which countries to recommend to EU governments -- who have final say -- next Tuesday in Strasbourg, but EU officials did not exclude the issue being settled at Thursday's meeting.
Crucial to the EU's wish to unite western and eastern Europe in a giant political and economic zone will be a waiting room to keep those countries excluded on track.
The Commissioners were to also to discuss setting up a standing European conference, which would keep all 10 eastern applicant countries involved and prepared for future membership at their own pace.

The plan to take in five new countries has a long list of supporters, including British Commissioners Sir Leon Brittan and Neil Kinnock, German Commissioner Martin Bangemann, Sweden's Commissioner Anita Gradin, Denmark's Ritt Bjerregaard and southern Commissioners like Greece's Christos Papoutis.
Several officials predicted that the Commission would finally come down in favour of opening talks with five eastern countries, plus Cyprus, after a struggle.

The backers say that if the EU is to honour its commitment to judge the applications by the eastern countries on objective criteria, Estonia and Slovenia should be admitted on the same basis as Poland.

But Commissioners from smaller countries, led by Santer, fear that by taking in five eastern countries the EU will commit itself to lengthy and difficult institutional reforms which could delay the enlargement and sap the power of the EU's smaller countries.

At the heart of the problem is the failure of EU leaders to agree at their June 16-17 Amsterdam Summit on the institutional reforms necessary to loosen up the bloc's decision-making procedures for the day it has up to a dozen new members.
Under the fudge agreed at Amsterdam the EU must hold a new treaty-revising conference if it expands to more than 20 members.
As Cyprus has already been in line for some time and is heavily backed by Greece, the number of EU members would expand to 21 if it was admitted along with five easterners.
